chapter: Early records, Detroit and Prohibition-era nightlife
title: Christmas 1928 with McKinney's Cotton Pickers in Detroit
summary: Using a downBeat article he wrote as notes, he recounts being recommended by Benny Carter to McKinney, earning $160 a week, and returning home after two weeks homesick.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Now, after the Rose Dance-land, did you then go to Benny Carter?
That's where I went after Rose Danceland?

Well, that's all I have. Maybe I left something out in the middle, maybe I didn't. But I have it that in the summer of '28 you were with Rose Danceland, and Morton, and then you went to Benny Carter's band in '29, sometime, at the Arcadia.

Well, you see, there's a break there, in the -- Christmas, 1928, I was out in Detroit with McKinney's Cotton Pickers. I went out there and -- hand me that envelope there, please. I don't want to get up because I've got this -- I brought my -- I figured I'd need this. This is a thing I wrote for downBeat some years ago.

Yeah, I went out to join McKinney's Cotton Pickers -- studio -- see, I always get the sequence of these things mixed up. They happened so fast. They happened so fast, you know, that -- quit Fletcher Henderson long before that.
I'll tell you, there was so much going on at one time.
Yeah. Fast and furious. You know, you'd stay on a job about two months, you know, and go to

another one. Yeah. Bamboo Inn. Yeah. Arcadia Ballroom. I assume this would be tenor player Joe Turner. Charlie Green and (Unintelligible) -- play one night in Baltimore with Duke Ellington. Oh, yes, I batted around after that and even played a one nighter in Baltimore with Duke Ellington.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, anyway, I -- when the -- this -- this job I got in Detroit with McKinney's Cotton Pickers, I wasn't working, and McKinney came to New York. Actually he came because he wanted to hire Benny Carter. So Benny Carter was involved with his own band and whatever, and he told McKinney, you know, about me. So I went out there and he hired me and -- for a lot of money in those days, more money than I'd ever made up till that time. Something like $160.00 a week. I had never made no money like that, you know. But I didn't stay long, because he had a very good job at the -- what the devil was the name of that ballroom? A ballroom in Detroit, anyway. (Greystone)
Yeah, I know which one you mean.
You know what I mean, yeah. And the reason I didn't stay was because that job closed and they were

-- again, I'd say they were going out on the road, you know. So the first stop was St. Louis. I said no, no, no. I'm going back home. So I only stayed there two weeks. I got there Christmas Day, for Christmas Day, 1928. I never will forget that, because the first time I'm away from home for Christmas, you know, and I'm sitting up in this coffee shop, eating ham and eggs, and they're playing Christmas carols, and the tears were running down my eyes. And I said, "What the hell am I doing out here in Detroit?" So I had a lot of fun, but I came back to New York. Then it was after that that I joined Benny Carter and jobs were always closing, and Benny's job closed too. And we were supposed to -- Benny's band -- and they closed about a month or two after I had joined his band, and the band supposedly was supposed to go back into the Arcadia Ballroom, but they never did.
